items.title: Simple circuits can create complex behaviors
items.content:
The world is full of surprising behavior: Beavers building dams, songbirds singing, spiders building webs, and you reading this article.

All of these behaviors are orchestrated by neurons firing in the brain. But how exactly do collections of neurons create these complex behaviors?

This is a huge question that researchers are still working on. But over the last half century, neuroscientists have solved some pieces of this puzzle.

In this article, we’ll build a tiny creature called a spark, and we’ll give it a very simple brain. As you’ll see, even this tiny brain can create rich and unexpected behaviors.

Suppose this spark feeds on light. Its goal in life is to reach the light.

The light-hungry spark needs a way to sense the world. So we’ll give it a rudimentary eye — a single neuron that detects brightness and converts it into electrical pulses.

It also needs a way to move. So we’ll give it another neuron that can wiggle a flipper.

By wiring the first sensory neuron to the second motor neuron , we’ve just assembled our first neural circuit:

With this simple circuit, the spark wiggles its flipper in proportion to the amount of light.

If the sparks happen to face the light, they’re drawn towards it. But most of the time, they miss.

Only a few paths cross the light. Clearly, we can do a lot better…

Here’s the problem: While the spark can speed up, it can’t steer. With one eye and one flipper, it only moves in one direction. But we need it to turn.

What if we give it another eye and flipper?

With two eyes, the spark can now sense whether the light is to its left or right. Now, it moves like this:

Hmm… that didn’t work. Instead of steering towards the light, it steered away from it!

If you didn’t know how their brains work, you might think that they fear light.

Why do they avoid the light? Well, if the light were to the spark’s left, then its left eye would sense more brightness, which means that its left flipper would wiggle faster, and this would cause it to turn right, away from the light. Conversely, if the light were to its right, then it would veer left.

But there’s a clever way to make this spark steer towards the light instead.

All we have to do is cross its connections. That is, we wire its left eye to its right flipper, and its right eye to its left flipper.

With this simple wiring change, it can finally steer towards the light.

But if you watch these sparks for a while, you’ll notice that there’s a problem.

While they can reach the light, they don’t slow down near it. Instead, they charge towards it like comets plunging towards the sun.

If you didn’t know how their brains work, now you might think that they’re attacking the light.

Why do they attack the light? The problem lies in the type of connection that we used.

To see why, we need to go back to our original spark. Remember how its flipper moved faster when the light got brighter? That’s because its eye and flipper were connected with an excitatory connection — where more input leads to more output.

If the light were a food source, then this spark would accelerate towards it, but it wouldn’t stop to enjoy its lunch.

Instead, we want the spark to slow down as it approaches the light. That is, we want its motion to be inhibited by light.

We can solve this by swapping out the excitatory connection for an inhibitory connection — one where more input leads to less output.

With the original excitatory connection, the spark overshoots the light. With the inhibitory one, it slows down and gently comes to a stop.

Now let’s bring back the original two-eyed spark, but this time with inhibitory connections between its eyes and flippers.

Now, the flipper closer to the light moves slower, while the flipper on the opposite side moves faster, and this makes the spark turn towards the light.

Hooray! It can finally steer to the light and come to a stop. You can move the light in the graphic above (or the one below) to watch the sparks react.

items.title: An LC-3 Disassembler in Haskell
items.content:
LC-3 assembly is an educational programming language. It is simple enough that complex programs can be written directly in it without needing a compiler, and thus it is often used in teaching assembly. An LC-3 textual assembly program is compiled to a binary object file by an assembler, and then executed by a virtual machine . Writing a virtual machine for LC-3 is a fun little exercise. However, in this post, we implement a disassembler for compiled LC-3 binaries back to textual assembly programs.

LC-3 assembly is an educational programming language. It is simple enough that complex programs can be written directly in it without needing a compiler, and thus it is often used in teaching assembly. An LC-3 textual assembly program is compiled to a binary object file by an assembler, and then executed by a virtual machine . Writing a virtual machine for LC-3 is a fun little exercise. However, in this post, we implement a disassembler for compiled LC-3 binaries back to textual assembly programs.

LC-3 has a simple instruction set with only 18 instructions. It works with eight 16-bit registers (numbered from 0 to 7), and 16-bit addressable memory. LC-3 instructions are also 16-bit, with first four bits used for opcodes, and the rest for instruction arguments.

There are instructions for doing arithmetic and bitwise logical operations, conditional branching, executing subroutines, loading from and storing to memory, handling interrupts and doing system calls. Some of them take source, destination, and base registers as arguments ( SR , DR , and BR respectively in the diagram above). Some other take integer immediate values, program counter, and address offsets ( imm , PCOffset , and offset respectively in the diagram above). The TRAP instruction take a code for the syscall to execute. Notice that we count the bits from left to right, zero-indexed.

When written in the textual assembly format, we use mnemonics for the opcodes and syscalls. The eight registers are written as R0 to R7 . The instructions can be labeled and referred from other instructions using them. Let’s start by looking at a simple LC-3 assembly file:

HW .STRINGZ "Hello World!" ; string data

As seen above, the assembly file can also contain assembler directives such as .STRINGZ , .FILL , .BLKW , .ORIG , and .END . Quoting the lc3asm docs:

tells the assembler where in memory to place the LC-3 program.

tells the assembler to set aside the next location in the program and initialize it with the value of the operand.

tells the assembler to set aside some number of sequential memory locations (BLocK of Words) in the program.

tells the assembler to initialize a sequence of n + 1 memory locations; the argument is a sequence of n characters, inside double quotation marks; the first n words of memory are initialized with the zero-extended ASCII codes of the corresponding characters in the string; the final word of memory is initialized to 0.

tells the assembler where the program ends; any characters that come after .END are ignored by the assembler.

We assemble the program with the lc3asm assembler, and then execute the resultant binary with the lc3 VM 1 :

It works as expected! As much fun as it would be to write an assembler and a VM, in this post, we don’t assemble or run LC-3 programs, we disassemble them. We don’t care what the instructions do, only how they are encoded.

Unlike an object file generated from X86 or Arm assembly, an LC-3 object file does not contain section tables separating code from data, symbol tables indicating function and variable names, relocation information, or debug symbols 2 . It contains only raw binary instructions and data that are freely intermixed in a single address space. This is made necessary by the fact that LC-3 has only 16-bit addressable memory. So data blocks and read-write memory addressed from code has to be within \(2^{16}\) bits or 8192 bytes of the code addressing it.

items.title: After Uber Destroyed Taxi Cabs, Drivers Now Face the Existential Threat of Self-Driving Cars: "It feels like every time I adjust to a new reality, another tech comes along & threatens my livelihood."
items.content:
In its first decade of existence, Uber managed to completely upend the decades-old taxi industry, shredding through million-dollar yellow cab dynasties and owner-operators alike. Now that those erstwhile cabbies have come to reluctant terms with the new algorithmic paradigm , self-driving cars are exploding onto the scene — pushing the workers who move America to their breaking point.

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, a coalition of worker advocacy groups and unions have come together to warn local lawmakers about the threat to their livelihoods, and to demand that the city take action to preserve drivers’ jobs.

According to Cambridge Daily , the group was made up of a newly organized App Drivers Union, which was joined by transit workers from Boston Carmen’s Union Local 589, and transportation and logistics workers from Teamster’s Local 25. They gathered in response to the rising presence of Waymo vehicles on Cambridge streets, which have begun mapping the roadways in obvious preparation for an eventual rollout of autonomous vehicles.

“I used to drive a cab, but lost my business to Uber,” said Abdazi Samantar, a local rideshare driver whose livelihood is now threatened by robotaxi companies like Waymo. “It feels like every time I adjust to a new reality, another technology comes along and threatens my livelihood.”

Whether Waymos literally takeover the role of rideshare drivers is maybe beside the point. Like the impact of apps like Uber and Lyft on cab drivers, robotaxis have a depressive effect on driver pay, leading to a gradual lessening of wages as competition for riders increases.

A case in point is Atlanta, where the local Rideshare Drivers Union has noted that workers have received lower pay, longer down-time between rides, and fewer overall fares since Waymo came to town in summer of 2025.

Though state officials across the US have mostly declined to allow municipal governments to enact labor protections for workers from rapidly-expanding robotaxi companies — let alone from exploitation by app giants like Uber — organizers in Atlanta have built a strong movement around practical economic demands.

For example, the ARDU has proposed a “robotaxi impact fee” of between $0.50 and $1.00 per ride, to be paid into a “driver transition fund” that would then offer alternative job training and financial assistance to struggling drivers. Reacting to driver demands, rideshare giants like Uber have come out in favor of limiting autonomous vehicles, putting additional pressure on local lawmakers to protect worker’s rights.

Whether rideshare workers in Cambridge can secure similar concessions remains to be seen, but the threat grows more acute with every street Waymo maps — meaning time is of the essence.

items.title: Memdoor: A team of 5 Qwen3.8-27B models beats Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard
items.content:
Five small models solve a programming problem together: a planner, two

ideators, a solver and a manager, plus a repair worker. Each starts from a

fresh context and talks only through files on disk. A script that runs the

samples decides success, not a model. It is the method of

Memdoor workflow: eight YAML files, no code, no model

The authors' harness rebuilt on the same model, Qwen3.8-27B, with their

prompts, loop and 128K reply cap. The first ten problems of their

LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes each, graded on every hidden test with

The authors' two columns are the regraded result files in their repository,

the numbers in their paper. Our column is

bench/results/parity-5pass/ : all 50 runs,

each with every request and reply, the program, the grader's output and the

cost. A run took a median of 40 minutes and $0.39; the 50 cost $35.79.

Ten problems, five passes, not the authors' 100. On a sample this small,

9.8 and 9.6 are the same number. The claim is parity with their harness, not

The contests date from spring 2025 and the model may have seen them in

training. Contamination cannot be ruled out, for any column.

Fable 5's column is one call per problem, from the authors' files. It was

The loop sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests.

The model ran on OpenRouter, not a local machine.

The one lost problem: the manager invented a wrong counterexample and the

team rewrote a correct program. Twice elsewhere a correct program was

overwritten and then recovered. Both gaps are the authors' loop, kept as is.

The parity check (every request byte for byte against their code), the hosts,

the changes it took and the first run's findings are in NOTES.md .

The same result, on one page: memdoor.ai/docs/team-solve .

curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash

memdoor connect openrouter # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt

# or no key: memdoor connect local (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio; Ollama needs a 32K window, not its 4K default)

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor

cp -r memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve ~/.memdoor/workflows/

cp -r ../memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve/sample/* . # task.md + tests/1.in … 5.out

memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait # exit 0 when every sample passes

For your own problem, replace task.md and put paired tests/N.in /

tests/N.out beside it. The program is solution.py , read from stdin,

compared to the samples with diff ; it needs Python 3 and bash. /workflow

The steps name no model: whatever /model is pinned to answers, a local one

To change a role, change its prompt in steps/ .

plan ──┬── ideate-a ──┬── solve ── test ── review ── repair ── verify

a proposal each: the most direct provable algorithm, and one from another family

the verdict: a nonzero exit fails the run

Every agent prompt says "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat".

The paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. Each step is one YAML

file in steps/ , in the format of mario ,

the engine underneath; requires: is the DAG.

Fable 5 측 결과는 문제당 한 번의 호출로 얻은 것이라고 한다. 본문이 중간에 끊겨 있다.

items.title: The support case of a customer who said that all they could see was a black screen
items.content:
If you hold a PC’s power button for 12 seconds, it will turn off at the hardware level without notifying the operating system. This is a safety feature so that you can turn of the computer even if the operating system’s “Shut down” command isn’t working.

After eight seconds of the power button being held down, the Windows kernel realizes that the user is trying to do a force-power-off of the system, and it quickly takes a kernel dump that can be uploaded to the Windows Error Reporting service the next time you turn the system on. (Sometimes four seconds isn’t enough time to get enough information, and the kernel dump is incomplete. I believe that on Windows Insider builds of Windows, you get a message that says something like “Please let go of the power button so we can collect more information, and then we will turn off the computer.” This gives the kernel more time to finish capturing its kernel dump.)

These emergency kernel dumps are internally classified as “long power button hold” (LPBH) failures. One of the pieces of information recorded in these emergency kernel dumps is whether the screen consists entirely of black pixels. Those failures are sub-classified as “black screen LPBH”, and they go to a special virtual team for analysis. (I happen to be a member of this black screen LPBH team.)

Sometimes the problem is a broken video driver. Sometimes the video driver is doing just fine, but the desktop compositor is just handing black pixels to the video driver. Sometimes the desktop compositor is doing just fine, but nobody is drawing anything to the screen. And those cases are further subdivided further into cases like “there is nobody around to draw anything” or “the person who normally draws stuff is hung.”

Back in the Windows 3.1 days, there was a customer product support call that would today have been classified as a “black screen” bug: The customer reported that they turned on the computer, and Windows started up, but when the logo went away, all they saw was a blank screen.

After some questioning, the customer support engineer put the story together: It turned out that this customer really liked the color black, so they decided to set up a goth theme. They set the wallpaper color to black. They set the title bar color to black. They set the button color to black. They set the window background color to black. They set the window text color to black. Every possible color you could pick in the Colors control panel was set to black.

Once you get yourself into this situation, it’s hard to get out because you can’t see anything.

I don’t know how the customer support engineer fixed the problem, but I’m guessing that they booted into MS-DOS, ran EDIT.COM , and deleted the [colors] section from the win.ini file , thereby returning all the system colors to defaults.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Statement: Denmark Continues its Work on Digital Sovereignty with Collabora Office
items.content:
Recent media coverage has raised questions about the status of a Danish government pilot project involving Collabora Office. We would like to provide some background, clarify what happened, and share our perspective on the continued work towards digital sovereignty in Denmark.

In 2025, the Danish Ministry of Digitization launched an initiative to explore alternatives to Microsoft productivity tools as part of its broader digital sovereignty strategy. The objective was not simply to replace one technology with another, but to establish greater freedom of choice and reduce dependency on individual technology providers.

The project was carried out in collaboration with the Danish software company cBrain , whose F2 platform is used across all Danish government ministries to support administrative processes, including case management, communication, document management, compliance, and archiving.

The first phase was successfully completed. Collabora Office was integrated with F2, demonstrating that individual users could freely switch between Collabora Office and Microsoft Office when editing documents, while maintaining their documents within the same government platform and using Microsoft-compatible document formats.

This was an important technical achievement, demonstrating how government organisations can introduce alternative productivity tools without replacing their underlying administrative systems.

Following the successful integration, the project entered a second phase, involving a larger group (around forty users) of ministry employees testing Collabora Office in their daily work.

As expected in a pilot of this nature, users identified functionality and compatibility issues requiring further refinement. Working directly with users, the project team collected feedback and continued improving the solution to address the specific requirements of Danish government workflows.

Initial issues with the pilot were leaked to the Danish press in December 2025. Senior Collabora Office engineers investigated and resolved the reported tickets. We were pleased to invest engineering and QA time in supporting the evaluation at our own expense, as we often do to serve our growing number of pilot accounts.

However, before this work could be completed, the Danish government was reorganised in June 2026, and the Ministry of Digitization was abolished as a standalone ministry. Its responsibilities and employees were transferred into a new ministerial structure.

As a consequence, the pilot lost its original organizational setting and was put on hold before the planned evaluation could be completed.

To our knowledge, no formal assessment of the final suitability of Collabora Office was completed, nor was a formal conclusion reached regarding the outcome of the pilot.

The interruption should therefore not be confused with a completed technical evaluation or a decision that the technology was unsuitable.

The interruption of the ministry’s pilot has recently attracted considerable media and political attention, including questions about Denmark’s progress towards digital sovereignty.

We welcome this interest in an important subject. At the same time, it is essential to distinguish between the interruption of an individual government project and the broader ambitions behind it.

The original technical integration was successful, valuable experience was gained through user testing, and the work provided a foundation for further development.

Most importantly, the underlying need has not changed. Governments across Europe continue to seek greater control over their digital infrastructure and the freedom to choose between technology providers.

We are pleased that the experience gained through the original pilot is now being carried forward through continued activities with other Danish public authorities, in collaboration with cBrain and its F2 platform.

items.title: It's the memory latency, stupid
items.content:
When you see your databases CPU at 100%, what is it actually doing? We like to act as though CPUs run code linearly for simplicity's sake, but in truth CPUs are incredibly complex beasts; they can potentially do many instructions at once, or sometimes none at all (despite our console showing 100%). Because CPUs can do so many things, one CPU at 100% may be doing much less than another at 100%. A CPU is considered "idle" only if no task (Linux task) needs CPU time; this does not mean the CPU itself is being fully saturated. So why would a CPU not be fully utilized, even if it appears to be at 100%?

Memory accesses are orders of magnitude slower than internal CPU operations. To give a good picture of how much so, a modern CPU might be able to process somewhere in the realm of 4-8 instructions per nanosecond. A memory access to RAM can take somewhere in the realm of 50-100ns. To ease your mathing, that means a modern CPU can do around 400-800 instructions for every one memory access from RAM.

up to a few hundred MB · ~50–100 instructions per access

Given this, CPUs are built from the ground up to work their way around this. The most obvious way this is dealt with is CPU caches. CPU caches keep memory closer to the CPU than RAM, literally baked into the CPU chip. The closest cache (the L1 cache) takes around 1ns per memory operation- that's 50-100x faster than RAM! The "problem" here of course is that the CPU caches are fairly small; the L1 cache for a modern CPU is probably around ~64KB, while the farther caches max out at a few hundred MB for top end processors. A good database tries manipulating data in small "chunks" to take full advantage of caches, and you'll often hear cache utilization as being one of the top concerns of performance engineering.

Let's look at GROUP BY aggregations to get a better grip on cache utilization. In GROUP BY, we're looking to take a dataset, group it by a certain column (or more), and perform certain aggregations (for example, count, or sum on another column). The "naive" method might be to open a HashTable keyed by the group key that grows ever larger. For every new row, you would check if that key exists- if it does, go to it's corresponding aggregation and update the result. Simple, right? The problem is that if you have millions of unique groups, you're not utilizing your cache at all! Nearly every HashTable access will be a "cold" hit that goes to RAM. This means that although your CPU may /look/ like it's 100% utilized, in truth it'll constantly be waiting for cold memory accesses.

To demonstrate this, we'll take our state-of-the-art Pivot engine and ravage it! We'll remove all our complex logic and replace it with simplicity:

_sender: & mut dyn Sender < RecordBatch >,

let group_keys = batch. column ( self .key_column). as_primitive ::< Int64Type >();

// If the Group Key doesn't exist- set it to 0

// Afterwards, add 1 to the group- this will give us a count(*) GROUP BY key_column

* self .counts. entry (key). or_insert ( 0 ) += 1 ;

items.summary_ko: 데이터베이스 CPU가 100%라고 해도 실제로는 계산이 쉬지 않고 돌아가는 상태가 아닐 수 있다. 리눅스에서 CPU가 '유휴'가 아니라는 것은 어떤 작업이 CPU 시간을 쓰고 있다는 뜻일 뿐, 명령을 꽉 채워 처리한다는 뜻은 아니다. 최신 CPU는 RAM 접근 한 번에 약 400~800개의 명령을 처리할 수 있을 만큼 메모리보다 훨씬 빠르다.
items.content_ko: 데이터베이스 CPU 사용률이 100%로 보여도 CPU가 실제로 무엇을 하는지는 다를 수 있다. CPU는 여러 명령을 동시에 처리하기도 하고, 아무 명령도 처리하지 않을 때도 있다. 리눅스에서 CPU가 '유휴' 상태가 아니라는 것은 어떤 작업이 CPU 시간을 요구한다는 뜻일 뿐, CPU가 완전히 포화되었다는 뜻은 아니다. 메모리 접근은 CPU 내부 연산보다 몇 자릿수나 느리다. 최신 CPU는 나노초당 약 4~8개의 명령을 처리할 수 있지만, RAM 접근에는 약 50~100나노초가 걸린다. 따라서 RAM 접근 한 번이 걸리는 동안 CPU는 약 400~800개의 명령을 처리할 수 있다. 이 격차를 줄이기 위해 CPU는 캐시 같은 구조를 사용한다. 본문이 중간에 끊겨 있어 캐시 이후의 내용은 확인할 수 없다.

items.title: Intel’s woes wipe out $1 trillion of semiconductor market cap in one day — PC market bloodbath leaves few chip stocks unscathed: $1 trillion in semiconductor market capitalization wiped out.
items.content:
Intel's shares plunged 30% on Friday, wiping out nearly $150 billion in market capitalization in a single day, the largest single-day loss in the company's history. The decline followed a disappointing financial outlook, largely driven by an anticipated drop of more than 20% in sales at Intel's client computing group (CCPG), the company's main cash cow. The declines quickly spread across the semiconductor industry. Although losses elsewhere were nowhere near as severe as Intel's, approximately $1 trillion in semiconductor market capitalization was wiped out on Friday, according to intraday estimates by Benzinga .

The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index (SOX), which tracks the stock performance of 30 major semiconductor companies, is one of the key indicators of the industry's financial health. On Friday, the index plunged 9.14%, or 1,052.82 points, to 10,465.38 points as of 2:31 PM ET, as Intel's disappointing outlook triggered a massive selloff across the semiconductor industry.

Intel was by far the biggest loser, as other chip-related stocks, while Arm (-12.68%), AMD (-12.48%), Qualcomm (-12.14%), Applied Materials (-8.73%), ASML (-8.13%), Lam Research (-8%), Micron (-7.28%), and Broadcom (-7.1%) suffered considerably less. Then again, while Nvidia lost 5.66% of its market cap, this translates to around $270 billion, which is a massive amount of money. Paradoxically, Nvidia lost more market capitalization in absolute dollar terms than Intel.

Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platforms

Intel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shape

Benchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the price

AMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent

In an unexpected turn of events, the downturn extended to server manufacturers and cloud giants too, as Dell (-12.67%), HPE (-8.10%), Supermicro (-6.96%), and Oracle (-6.88%) lost nearly 7% to 13% of their value. Reuters noted that investors increasingly question the scale of capital investments required to expand AI infrastructure as well as the sustainability of that spending.

Intel’s client computing and physical AI group (CCPG) generated $8.1 billion in revenue during Q3 2026, down 5% year-over-year and 9% sequentially. Weaker demand and increased competition reduced client processor shipments by 14% year-over-year, which was partially offset by a 9% increase in average selling prices. CCPG accounted for nearly half of Intel's revenue of around $16.5 billion and the company's main source of cash. As strong demand for server processors only partially offsets declining client sales, Intel guided its Q4 revenue to be between $15 billion and $16 billion.

Intel expects the client market to deteriorate further in Q4 2026 and into 2027 as elevated memory prices and shortages of other components impact PC prices and demand. In general, Intel expects the client PC market to decline 10% in 2027 compared to 2026, which will inevitably have an effect on CCPG performance. While Intel expects its data center business to continue growing in 2027, industry-wide supply constraints will limit its ability to fully capitalize on demand.

2026 has been a mixed bag for Intel so far. On the one hand, the company achieved its highest market capitalization ever — $673.43 billion in mid-June — on growing sales of data center CPUs, strong sales of client products, and a return to profitability (if the $12.5 billion non-cash accounting charge associated with shares issued to the U.S. government is excluded). On the other hand, the company's capitalization has dropped by nearly 50% to $338.91 billion since mid-June (with $148.68 billion in just one day), as investors began to realize that the performance of Intel's CCPG heavily depends on memory prices, as customers and businesses tend not to like overpriced systems. items.title: How hard is it to check for whitespace?
items.content:
By Sergey Tselovalnikov on 30 October 2026

When looking through a piece of source code recently, I stumbled across this method from Guava – a popular Java library from Google.

As you might've guessed from the name, this method checks whether a given character is a whitespace character. Yet the code looks a lot more complex than a simple c == ' ' check. This made me curious and sent me down a small rabbit hole trying to understand where all this complexity was coming from. If you're curious how this code works too, this article is for you.

The first thing one needs when inspecting a function that checks whether a character is whitespace is to define what whitespace actually is. While the SPACE (U+0020) is probably the best-known whitespace character, it's not the only one. If you've been writing code for a while, you can probably name a few more – the non-breaking space NO-BREAK SPACE (U+00A0) , a tab CHARACTER TABULATION (U+0009) , a newline LINE FEED (U+000A) .

Well, there are more. Unicode defines a White_Space property that gives us a list of 25 characters. Here they are – meticulously copied ,

, , , , ,, , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ,　 .

Each of these characters has a different purpose. FIGURE SPACE (U+2007) , for example, has the same width as a digit in a table, while THIN SPACE (U+2009) and HAIR SPACE (U+200A) provide progressively smaller gaps. NO-BREAK SPACE (U+00A0) has the width of an ordinary space, but keeps the surrounding text together when wrapping a line.

It's not always easy to tell whether a character is in the whitespace set from the name or by looking at the glyph either. For instance, ZERO WIDTH SPACE (U+200B) isn't a whitespace character at all. Despite the name, it's a format character that can indicate a word or line break opportunity without adding a visible gap.

There are also some less obvious members of the set too. OGHAM SPACE MARK (U+1680) can actually be rendered as a visible horizontal line. In Ogham fonts with a stemline, the space continues that line between letters (e.g. ᚛ᚆᚓᚂᚂᚑ ᚒᚑᚏᚂᚇ᚜), while in stemless fonts, it's blank. So even the assumption that whitespace must look empty isn't always true.

Having a single definition of whitespace is only useful if everyone can agree on it. But even within a single runtime, some libraries might disagree on what whitespace is.

Consider the NO-BREAK SPACE (U+00A0) I mentioned above. It's included in Unicode's White_Space property, but Java explicitly excludes it , along with two other non-breaking spaces. The javadoc usefully highlights that the method checks for whitespace according to Java , rather than according to the Unicode property we had a look at before.

Character.isWhitespace( '\u00A0' ); // false

But what about other runtimes? Looking at two more popular ones, Python and JavaScript, we can see that there isn't a single authoritative list of characters everyone agrees on. Python, for example, has a convenient str.isspace() method. And unlike Java, it considers U+00A0 a whitespace character.

So possibly Python just follows Unicode's White_Space property? Not quite.

The interesting one here is FILE SEPARATOR (U+001C) . It's an ASCII control character originally intended to separate pieces of information, and it isn't included in Unicode's White_Space property. So Python recognises 29 whitespace characters, rather than Unicode's 25.

JavaScript takes yet another approach. It doesn't have an equivalent of the Character.isWhitespace() method, but we can use the \s character class in a regular expression:

The odd one out above is NEXT LINE (U+0085) . Unicode explicitly includes it in White_Space , and Python accepts it too, but JavaScript doesn't. Instead, JavaScript recognises ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE (U+FEFF) , which Unicode doesn't include in the set.

I haven't looked through any other runtimes, but something tells me the inconsistencies won't stop at these three.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.content_ko: 보안 연구자 Nightmare-Eclipse가 공개한 YellowKey 제로데이 취약점은 물리적 접근만으로 Windows 11 기본 BitLocker 보호를 우회할 수 있다. items.title: Sam Altman Says Gen Z Are Lame for Not Worshipping AI: "They always want to go do the thing that was cool five years ago."
items.content:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman sympathizes with Gen Zers entering the job market. It’s just unfortunate that the AI tools he’s responsible for ushering into the world are completely upending the nature of work and finding a job.

“It’s totally true that huge numbers of tasks that people do today will be done better, cheaper, and faster by AI — and completely differently,” Altman said in an interview with Stanford’s Graduate School of Business, as quoted by Fortune .

This, according to Altman, actually presents an opportunity. He argues that all the tumult caused by AI is a good thing, as it gives ambitious Gen Zers who are willing to embrace AI an opportunity to catapult their careers or launch a business.

“I think you want to be starting your career at a time of the highest degree of change,” Altman said.

He then dissed Gen Zers who aren’t getting with the times.

“My chronic disappointment with MBA students is that they always want to go do the thing that was cool five years ago and not do the new thing,” Altman said. “I think this is a great time to go do the new thing.”

But the interviewer pointed out the obvious flaw in Altman’s logic.

“So go do the new thing, even if AI is the cool thing right now,” she said almost incredulously, eliciting a roar of laughter from the crowd.

The thing is, AI isn’t that far away from being what was “cool five years ago.” The excitement that bubbled from ChatGPT’s release in November 2022, and the wave of AI optimism in the year that followed, feels like it happened a lifetime ago. After that, public opinion on AI quickly began to sour. Artists and tastemakers certainly didn’t embrace it. But businesses rapidly integrated AI tools in an effort to economize their operations, automate tasks , surveil workers , and justify layoffs .

In short, AI is no longer “cool,” if it ever was. It’s now an inescapable part of our reality. Basically every programmer uses AI at work. Jobseekers are interviewed by AI models.

It’s so pervasive now that even tech founders are getting sick of it; Paul Graham, the cofounder of startup accelerator Y Combinator, acted as a weathervane when he said that he views AI writing in the pitches he receives as a sign of laziness.

items.title: 사생활침해 범죄가 의심 됩니다. 도움이 필요합니다
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.content_ko: Gitea의 OAuth2 userinfo 엔드포인트(/login/oauth/userinfo)는 groups 클레임을 공개 조직으로 제한할지 판단할 때, 요청을 인증한 자격 증명의 범위 대신 Authorization 헤더를 OAuth2 액세스 토큰으로 다시 파싱했다. 공개 전용 OAuth2 토큰을 쿼리 파라미터나 폼 필드로 보내거나, 공개 전용 개인 액세스 토큰을 사용하면 그 범위가 비어 있는 것으로 처리됐다. 그 결과 클레임에 토큰 소유자의 비공개 조직, 팀, 숨겨진 멤버십이 포함됐다. 노출되는 정보는 소유자의 조직과 팀 이름, 멤버십으로 제한되며 저장소 내용은 노출되지 않는다. 수정 후 엔드포인트는 인증에 쓰인 토큰의 범위를 사용한다. 원격 악용 가능 여부는 False로 표기되어 있다.
